children: Crude oil futures fell for the third time in four sessions on Thursday as news of U.S. efforts to engage Iranian hardliners in talks offset some concerns over persistent Middle East supply risks and the possibility of renewed military escalation.
Vice President Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, in an effort to revive peace negotiations,
"In my opinion, the administration is finally talking to the right person," as Rezaei's position is "probably second only to Iran's Supreme Leader," Mizuho's Robert Yawger said in a note.

But Iran-backed Houthi militants said Thursday they attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the Rabigh oil refinery, an Aramco facility in ​Abqaiq, and airports in the country; Saudi officials have not confirmed the strikes.
The reports of new Houthi attacks and claims by Iran that four oil tankers had struck sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz helped oil recoup some losses later in the session.
The oil market is awaiting further news as a U.S. peace deal remains on the table, although "most traders still feel escalation of war is likely coming," BOK Financial's Dennis Kissler wrote.
Some expectations of rising crude and diesel production from Russia may have helped keep ​a lid on prices.

No confirmed attacks on Russian refining infrastructure have occurred since the October 15 strike on the Ryazan refinery, J.P. Morgan analysts said, and "the silence has allowed Russian refinery runs to ⁠rebound by ​350K bbl/day last week, to 4M bbl/day."
